name: Machine Learning Foundations to Practice
summary: A structured route from first principles to models you can defend: learning theory, linear models, deep learning mechanics, and the discipline of honest evaluation.
description:
This path assumes no prior machine learning but does assume you can differentiate a function and multiply matrices. It moves in four stages: what learning is and why generalization is the whole problem; the classical model families and the optimization underneath them; the mechanics of deep networks, derived rather than memorised; and finally the evaluation and deployment discipline that separates a notebook from a system.

Every stage names its topics, and every topic in this platform carries prerequisites, key results, common misconceptions and further reading with real citations. Work the topics in the order given — the prerequisite graph is not decorative, and skipping ahead is the most common way to end up memorising formulas you cannot derive.
audience: Self-directed learners with calculus and linear algebra who want a rigorous grounding rather than an API tour
objectives: Formulate any supervised problem as minimisation of population risk and explain what the empirical proxy costs you.
Derive and implement least squares, gradient descent, and the bias-variance decomposition from first principles.
Explain backpropagation as reverse-mode automatic differentiation and state its cost relative to forward mode.
Derive scaled dot-product attention, including the 1/sqrt(d) factor, masking, and the key-value cache.
Design an evaluation protocol that does not leak, and report results that a reviewer could reproduce.
prerequisitesNote: Single-variable calculus, matrix multiplication, and basic probability. No programming framework is assumed, though the exercises use Python and NumPy.
completionCriteria: Complete both flagship courses, reach at least 'practising' mastery on every core topic in the path, and score 70% or more of the Problem Arena points for those topics.
outcomeNote: You will be able to read a machine learning paper's method section and identify what is derived, what is assumed, and what is merely reported — and to build a model whose claimed performance survives an honest evaluation.

stages.title: Stage 1 — What learning is
stages.summary: Risk, generalization, and the vocabulary every later stage depends on.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Classical models and the optimization under them
stages.summary: Linear and generalized linear models, convexity, duality, and why step size decides whether you converge at all.

stages.title: Stage 3 — How deep networks learn
stages.summary: Automatic differentiation, signal propagation, initialization, and normalization — the mechanics that make depth trainable.

stages.title: Stage 4 — The transformer and training dynamics
stages.summary: Attention, block conventions, optimizers and schedules, then the evaluation discipline that makes results trustworthy.

name: Deep Learning Research Track
summary: For learners who can already train a network and want the mathematical and systems depth to read, reproduce, and critique current research.
description:
This path starts where the foundations path ends. It assumes you have implemented backpropagation, trained a transformer, and run a cross-validated evaluation. Its purpose is to convert engineering familiarity into research literacy: the theory that says when a method should work, the systems knowledge that says what it actually costs, and the critical reading habits that separate a reproducible result from a favourable benchmark.

The stages are ordered by dependency, not by popularity. Representation and optimization theory come first because everything downstream assumes them; architecture theory follows; then the systems and evaluation layer that determines whether any of it can be trained at scale and believed.
audience: Graduate students, research engineers, and practitioners preparing to read and reproduce conference papers
objectives: Explain the infinite-width and neural tangent kernel limits and state honestly what they do and do not predict about finite networks.
Analyse loss landscapes, grokking, and double descent, distinguishing established results from open interpretation.
Derive the cost and memory profile of attention variants and explain why sub-quadratic methods trade expressiveness for scaling.
Reason about distributed and memory-parallel training: what is sharded, what is replicated, and where the communication bottleneck sits.
Critique a paper's evaluation: baselines, ablations, seeds, compute budget, and whether the claimed effect survives them.
prerequisitesNote: Both flagship courses, or equivalent: backpropagation derived by hand, attention implemented, and a cross-validated evaluation you have run yourself.
completionCriteria: Reach 'practising' or higher mastery on at least 12 topics in this path, and complete a written critique of one recent paper using the evaluation checklist in Stage 4.
outcomeNote: You will be able to enter a new subfield, locate its canonical results, identify which claims are derived and which are empirical regularities, and design an experiment that would actually test a contested claim.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Theory of representation and optimization
stages.summary: The infinite-width limits, loss landscapes, and nonconvex optimization theory behind why deep networks train at all.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Architecture theory
stages.summary: Attention beyond the quadratic baseline, normalization mathematics, and the geometry of equivariant architectures.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Systems: what it actually costs
stages.summary: Memory, parallelism, and the serving constraints that decide which architectures survive contact with scale.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Reading research critically
stages.summary: Evaluation methodology, ablation discipline, reproducibility, and the honest classification of claims.
